cross_item_rule.rule: The only rule that repeated: when the stem itself names the mechanism or variable under test, prefer the option whose predicate lies on that same axis (motor rehearsal -> the motor task; browsing -> its hydrological alternative; survival -> a reserved function). It selected a pick on 3 items (1, 16, 23) and justified an actual elimination on exactly one (1). It did NOT generalize: on the 2x2 and quantity-permutation items (4, 6) every option sits on the named axis, so the rule is silent there, and on the 8 vocab/word-choice items there is no axis at all. A second, weaker rule fired once: logical subsumption between two options (18), where one option entails another and therefore cannot be the unique key.

shared_frames.note: Permutation frames: every option is one sentence with one or two variables swapped (which gap / which surface x which direction / how much of the gap and by what). Solving one tells you nothing about another, but they share the property that the option set alone carries no content - these are the cleanest items in the batch.

Text-1/Text-2 rebuttal frame: each offers three causal confounds plus one measurement-validity objection. Knowing the frame does not decide any of them; it does warn that picking 'the measurement one' every time would be a tell if the keys clustered there.
Bare word-choice completions with no stem content. Four unrelated adjectives each; all four legal by construction.
Word-in-context, all four options attested senses of the headword. Structurally identical and uniformly undecidable blind.

Long-option purpose/function/structure frame: all options share a fixed opening clause and differ only in the trailing completion. One item cannot help another, but the shared stem clause means any elimination has to come from the trailing clause alone.
